subChunks.title: Change Data Capture and Event Streaming
subChunks.hookHtml: Every database change is an event. Change Data Capture (CDC) turns the database's WAL into a stream of events — enabling real-time data synchronisation, audit trails, and event-driven architectures without polling.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is CDC

CDC captures every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE as it happens and makes it available to downstream consumers — message queues, search indexes, data warehouses, or other databases — in near real-time.

PostgreSQL logical replication

-- Enable logical decoding:
wal_level = logical  -- in postgresql.conf

-- Create a publication (what to publish):
CREATE PUBLICATION my_pub
  FOR TABLE apprentices, quest_completions;

-- Create a subscription (on the subscriber database):
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION my_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=primary port=5432 dbname=arcane user=replicator'
  PUBLICATION my_pub;

Debezium — CDC via Kafka

Debezium is the standard open-source CDC tool. It reads PostgreSQL WAL via a replication slot and publishes change events to Kafka topics:

-- Event payload format (simplified):
{
  "op": "u",  -- operation: c=create, u=update, d=delete
  "before": { "id": 1, "xp": 1200 },
  "after":  { "id": 1, "xp": 1300 },
  "source": { "table": "apprentices", "lsn": "...", "ts_ms": 1234567890 }
}

Use cases

  • Search index sync — keep Elasticsearch in sync with the database without polling
  • Cache invalidation — invalidate Redis cache entries when a row changes
  • Data warehouse ETL — stream changes to BigQuery/Snowflake in near real-time
  • Audit log — complete immutable record of all database changes
  • Microservice events — emit events to other services without dual-write

Replication slot lag

CDC uses replication slots. If the consumer (Kafka connector) falls behind, the slot accumulates WAL — potentially filling disk. Monitor pg_replication_slots:

SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(
  pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS lag
FROM pg_replication_slots;

storyBeats.text: The search index is always 30 seconds stale. The polling job hammers the database. There is a better way.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: CDC turns your database into an event source. Every change is published as it happens — no polling, no load, always current. Debezium reads the WAL as a first-class replication consumer. The database does not even know it is being observed. Watch your replication slot lag — a stalled consumer can fill your disk with WAL.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 CDC architecture design

Design a CDC pipeline for this scenario: whenever an apprentice's XP changes, update their record in an Elasticsearch search index within 1 second, without the database or API knowing about Elasticsearch.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Architecture: PostgreSQL → Debezium → Kafka → Elasticsearch Sink Connector

1. PostgreSQL configuration:
   wal_level = logical
   CREATE PUBLICATION xp_changes FOR TABLE apprentices;

2. Debezium Kafka Connector reads the apprentices publication and publishes to Kafka topic 'db.arcane.apprentices' for every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

3. Kafka topic receives events like:
   { 'op': 'u', 'after': { 'id': 1, 'name': 'Alice', 'xp': 1300 } }

4. Elasticsearch Kafka Sink Connector reads from 'db.arcane.apprentices' and upserts into ES index 'apprentices' using document ID = apprentice.id.

Why this decouples concerns:
- The database does not write to ES directly (no dual-write, no ES failures breaking writes)
- The API does not know about ES
- ES is eventually consistent with the database (typically < 1 second lag)
- If ES goes down, events queue in Kafka — no data loss, Debezium replays from WAL on recovery

Replication slot monitoring:
SELECT slot_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS lag
FROM pg_replication_slots;
Alert if lag > 100MB.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the outbox pattern: how it solves the dual-write problem without CDC infrastructure, and what its trade-offs are versus Debezium.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The dual-write problem: you want to write to the database AND send an event to a message queue. If the DB write succeeds but the event send fails (or vice versa), your systems are inconsistent.

Outbox pattern: instead of writing to the queue directly, write an event record to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business data.

Transactions: BEGIN; UPDATE apprentices SET xp = 1300 WHERE id = 1; INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload) VALUES ('apprentices', '...'); COMMIT;

A separate background process (or Debezium on the outbox table) reads from outbox and publishes to the message queue. Once published, mark the outbox row as processed (or delete it).

Vs Debezium: the outbox is simpler — no CDC infrastructure needed. Any database can support it. The message schema is explicitly controlled by the application.

Trade-offs: the outbox adds a table write to every transaction. The background publisher adds latency (typically 100ms-1s). Debezium is lower-latency (milliseconds) and captures all changes including those not explicitly outboxed, but requires Kafka and Debezium infrastructure.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what Change Data Capture is, how it works with the WAL, and describe one concrete use case where CDC is better than polling.

options: The process of streaming every database INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE as events to downstream consumers in near real-time
A method of logging all SQL queries for auditing
A way to replicate an entire database to a standby
A backup strategy that captures incremental changes daily
questions.answer: The process of streaming every database INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE as events to downstream consumers in near real-time
questions.explanation: CDC treats every database change as an event. Tools like Debezium read the WAL and publish change events to message queues. Downstream consumers (search indexes, warehouses, caches) subscribe to the event stream.

questions.prompt: Why is CDC better than polling for keeping a search index in sync?
options: CDC captures every change in real-time without load on the database; polling adds a recurring query load and may miss changes between polls
CDC is more reliable because it uses a dedicated connection
Polling cannot detect deletes; CDC can
CDC is faster because it uses indexes; polling does not
questions.answer: CDC captures every change in real-time without load on the database; polling adds a recurring query load and may miss changes between polls
questions.explanation: A polling query (SELECT * FROM t WHERE updated_at > last_poll) runs periodically, adds load, may have clock skew issues, and cannot reliably detect deletes without soft-delete flags. CDC reads the WAL — it captures every change with zero polling overhead.

questions.prompt: A CDC consumer (Debezium) is stopped for maintenance for 12 hours. What happens to the replication slot?
options: WAL accumulates in the replication slot for 12 hours — potentially filling disk if WAL generation is high
Changes are lost — CDC cannot backfill
The slot is automatically dropped after 1 hour
PostgreSQL pauses writes until the consumer reconnects
questions.answer: WAL accumulates in the replication slot for 12 hours — potentially filling disk if WAL generation is high
questions.explanation: Replication slots hold WAL until the consumer confirms it has processed the events. A paused consumer lets WAL accumulate. On a high-write database this can fill disk in hours. Monitor pg_replication_slots lag and set a disk alert.

questions.prompt: A team wants to update their search index when orders change, but has no Kafka infrastructure. What is the simplest correct approach?
options: Outbox pattern — write events to an outbox table in the same transaction; a simple background worker reads and publishes them
Direct dual-write — write to the database and search index in the same code
A cron job that polls the orders table every minute
A database trigger that calls an HTTP endpoint
questions.answer: Outbox pattern — write events to an outbox table in the same transaction; a simple background worker reads and publishes them
questions.explanation: The outbox pattern provides transactional event publishing without Kafka infrastructure. The outbox table is in the same database — the event is written atomically with the business data. A simple background worker publishes and marks events as processed. Dual-write is unreliable (partial failure). HTTP in a trigger is dangerous. Polling is inefficient and misses deletes.
